title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
challenge_note: Highest oxygen tests in microgravity (up to 85% O2 in inverse flames); relevant to Moon Base atmospheres.
objective:
1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
hypothesis:
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
  5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
research_impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.  The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

findings.conditions_text: Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K
findings.statement: At representative values of L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, the Richardson number for a spherical diffusion flame is 1300 in normal gravity; the report concludes that typical spherical diffusion flames require microgravity to make buoyancy negligible.
findings.source_quote: Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude.

findings.conditions_text: approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity
findings.statement: Analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free microgravity below 10-5 g is needed for spherical diffusion flames to approach quasi-steady state.
findings.source_quote: Our analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames.

findings.conditions_text: after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames
findings.statement: In CFI-G tests, non-premixed cool flames occurred after normal hot flames self-extinguished, but their presence was not recognized during testing and the tests were terminated, shortening cool-flame combustion.
findings.safety_implication: Fire monitoring and test procedures that detect only hot flames could miss ongoing low-temperature combustion after apparent flame extinction.
findings.equipment_implication: Detection systems and operating procedures should account for cool flames persisting after hot-flame extinction.
findings.source_quote: Meanwhile, evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the testing. During that testing, it wasn’t known that the cool flames were present after hot flame extinction and the tests were terminated, which unknowingly and sadly shortened the duration of the cool flame combustion.

findings.conditions_text: normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39
findings.quantity: conditions for observing spherical cool diffusion flames
findings.statement: Normal n-butane spherical cool diffusion flames were observed on the ISS only at 2 bar and an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39; the flames were not readily produced.
findings.source_quote: Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39.

findings.conditions_text: cool diffusion flames burning near the surface of fuel pools
findings.statement: Cool diffusion flames burning near the surface of liquid n-heptane pools had measured peak temperatures of 705–760 K, corresponding to a 70 K gas-temperature increase; autoignition first occurred at 550 K.
findings.source_quote: The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, which corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Autoignition first occurred at 550 K.

findings.conditions_text: during Increments 64-66
findings.statement: During the CFI-G ISS experiment, researchers identified 15 cool flames among tests that ignited 280 hot flames using ethane, propane, and n-butane.
findings.source_quote: A total of 280 hot flames were ignited (or in some cases naturally reignited) for the CFI-G experiment during Increments 64-66, where 33, 225, and 22 flames were ignited in the three increments, respectively. Testing began near the end of Increment 64 and the final test day was conducted at the start of Increment 66. Cool flame evidence was seen in some tests and 15 cool flames, listed and discussed later, have been identified thus far.

findings.conditions_text: 30 vol% n-butane and 40 vol% O2, normal flames, a pressure of 2.03 bar, and mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s
findings.quantity: conditions under which cool diffusion flames were observed
findings.statement: In the ISS tests, cool diffusion flames from 30 vol% n-butane occurred only with 40 vol% O2, normal flames, a pressure of 2.03 bar, and mass flow rates between 0.75 and 1.5 mg/s.
findings.equipment_implication: These observed conditions can inform atmosphere-control studies, but the reported tests do not establish general flammability limits.
findings.source_quote: These cool flames were observed only with the following conditions: a) concentrations of 30 vol% n-butane and 40 vol% O2, b) normal flames, c) a pressure of 2.03 bar, and d) mass flow rates between 0.75 – 1.5 mg/s.

findings.conditions_text: in microgravity compared to normal gravity
findings.statement: For ACME CLD Flame, dilution limits were extended in microgravity compared with normal gravity.
findings.safety_implication: Spacecraft fire-safety assessments should account for the possibility that flames can persist at greater dilution in microgravity than normal-gravity tests indicate.
findings.equipment_implication: Atmosphere-control thresholds based on normal-gravity dilution limits may not ensure flame prevention in microgravity.
findings.source_quote: Early results show that the dilution limits are extended in microgravity compared to normal gravity.

findings.conditions_text: Steady microgravity flames
findings.statement: Steady microgravity flames in ACME CLD Flame were more stable and had lower lift-off heights than normal-gravity flames, attributed to the lack of buoyancy.
findings.safety_implication: Fire-risk evaluations for spacecraft should not rely on normal-gravity expectations for flame stability or lift-off behavior.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew procedures and fire-response assumptions should account for the greater stability and lower lift-off of steady microgravity flames.
findings.source_quote: Steady microgravity flames are also more stable and have lower lift-off heights due to the lack of buoyancy.

findings.conditions_text: so far have not been observed in CFI-G testing
findings.statement: In CFI-G testing to date, gaseous-fuel cool diffusion flames had not been observed.
findings.source_quote: CFI-G’s goal is to study non-premixed cool flames using gaseous fuels, which have not been observed before and so far have not been observed in CFI-G testing.

findings.conditions_text: at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogen-diluted butane fuel
findings.statement: Nitrogen-diluted butane flames at 2 atm produced non-premixed cool flames after the hot flames quenched; the cool flames were detected through thermal radiation and burner-temperature measurements.
findings.safety_implication: Cool flames can persist after a hot flame quenches, so flame-out indications based only on visible heat or light may not establish that combustion has ended.
findings.equipment_implication: Fire detection intended to confirm flame extinction should account for faint post-quench cool-flame emissions or associated thermal signals.
findings.source_quote: These tests were performed at a chamber pressure of 2 atm with nitrogen-diluted butane fuel. Cool flames give off little heat or light and were too faint to be visible real time during testing. But their presence was revealed by thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements after the hot flames quenched.
findings.earth_application: Vehicle-engine ignition and combustion design may benefit from understanding gaseous-fuel cool-flame chemistry.

findings.conditions_text: inverse flames; heat loss to the burner’s supply tube
findings.statement: In inverse flames, heat loss to the burner supply tube locally quenched the flame and created an opening where reactants mixed; the opening could oscillate and grow until extinction, although some flames remained quasi-steady despite it.
findings.safety_implication: Localized heat loss can trigger progressive flame instability and extinction, so flame persistence cannot be inferred from an initially sustained spherical flame alone.
findings.equipment_implication: Burner and feed-tube thermal design can affect flame stability and extinction behavior.
findings.source_quote: These flames are locally quenched by heat loss to the burner’s supply tube leaving an opening in the flame. The opening, which allows reactant mixing, often oscillates in size while growing until the flame fully extinguishes. In some tests the extinction occurs abruptly, but in others the oscillations can last for tens of seconds.

findings.conditions_text: inverse propane flames; fourth day of testing
findings.statement: The investigators had not observed evidence of cool flames with inverse propane flames after four days of testing.
findings.source_quote: This day was our fourth day of testing with inverse propane flames, and we have yet to see evidence of cool flames with this fuel.

findings.conditions_text: extra day of testing with normal flames
findings.statement: During the final normal-flame butane tests, cool flames occurred between hot-flame episodes, enabling the extinguished hot flames to reignite repeatedly.
findings.safety_implication: An apparently extinguished hot flame may not indicate that combustion has ceased if cool-flame reactions can continue and trigger reignition.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew response procedures should account for possible reignition after a hot flame appears to extinguish.
findings.source_quote: In two tests, the butane hot flames extinguished due to radiative heat loss, but then seconds later they reignited. This extinction and reignition occurred several times during each of these tests. The butane reignited because a cool flame occurred between the hot flames.
findings.earth_application: The finding may inform vehicle-engine ignition research, where the report notes cool-flame chemistry is relevant to ignition.

findings.conditions_text: in microgravity; nearly impossible to create in Earth’s gravity
findings.statement: Cool diffusion flames burning gaseous fuels were created in microgravity, while creating such flames in Earth gravity is described as nearly impossible.
findings.safety_implication: This result alone does not establish that ordinary gaseous-fuel fires are more likely or harder to control in spacecraft.
findings.source_quote: Cool flames were first discovered aboard the space station in 2012 burning liquid fuel; more recently, the investigation created cool flames burning gaseous fuels.
findings.earth_application: The investigation may improve understanding of combustion and fires on Earth.

findings.conditions_text: with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert
findings.statement: The report states that n-pentane testing was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated Rack and ACME chamber insert because of its low vapor pressure, so ethane was used as an alternate.
findings.source_quote: In contrast to objective 2 (and hypothesis 3), it was not feasible with the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and ACME chamber insert to conduct tests with n-pentane as proposed (because of its low vapor pressure) and testing was instead conducted with ethane as an alternate.

findings.conditions_text: during ACME testing
findings.statement: ACME spherical burners did not always produce spherically symmetric flames, reportedly because of excess flow through the porous-sphere joint and local flame quenching from heat loss to the support tube.
findings.source_quote: Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local flame quenching.

findings.conditions_text: two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition; closest thermocouple approximately 1 cm from burner surface
findings.statement: In two CFI-G tests with the long/near thermocouple, a platinum-containing exposed type-B thermocouple about 1 cm from the burner surface contributed to rapid reignition during intervening low-temperature combustion, limiting its duration.
findings.safety_implication: Hot, exposed platinum-containing components near fuel flames may catalyze oxidation and undermine flame-extinction assumptions.
findings.equipment_implication: Avoid placing exposed platinum-containing thermocouples near the burner when evaluating whether low-temperature combustion persists after hot-flame quenching.
findings.source_quote: In later testing with the long/near thermocouple, two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening low-temperature combustion. It appears that the closest thermocouple, approximately 1 cm from the burner surface, was a factor in the reignition. The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons.

findings.conditions_text: normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39
findings.quantity: hot flame size relative to cool diffusion flame size
findings.statement: The hot flames that spawned spherical n-butane cool diffusion flames were 2.6 times as large as the cool diffusion flames.
findings.source_quote: The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large.

findings.conditions_text: observed spherical cool diffusion flames
findings.statement: Observed spherical cool diffusion flames resided in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53.
findings.source_quote: They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53.

findings.conditions_text: homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism
findings.statement: Cantera autoignition simulations using the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool-flame temperature of 885 K for homogeneous mixtures, significantly higher than the observed temperatures.
findings.source_quote: Cantera autoignition simulations for homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool flame temperature of 885 K, which is significantly higher than observed.

findings.conditions_text: The first three days of testing
findings.statement: During the first three days of ISS CFI-G testing, the team found no evidence that self-sustained cool flames had been created, although momentary cool flames could not be ruled out.
findings.source_quote: The first three days of testing have yielded dozens of flames, some lasting several minutes. Based on the output from the photomultipliers, radiometers, and intensified camera images we do not believe any self-sustained cool flames were created.

findings.quantity: radiant heat flux behavior and hot-cool flame transitions
findings.statement: After a hot n-butane diffusion flame underwent radiative extinction, radiant heat flux remained above zero while fuel continued flowing, indicating a cool flame; some tests then experienced repeated hot-flame reignition.
findings.safety_implication: A drop in radiant output after hot-flame extinction may not mean combustion has ended, so fire monitoring should account for persistent low-level emission and possible reignition.
findings.equipment_implication: Radiant monitoring and response procedures should consider persistent emission after apparent hot-flame extinction and the possibility of reignition.
findings.source_quote: Unlike the heat flux shown in Fig. 1(a), Fig. 1(b) shows that the radiant heat flux did not drop to zero after the radiative extinction of a hot flame. Instead, it decreased to a certain level and stayed at that level until the fuel stopped flowing. Figure 1(c) shows multiple hot-cool flame transitions.
findings.earth_application: Radiant monitoring for fires could account for continued combustion and reignition after visible flames diminish.

findings.quantity: relative reaction-zone breadth and flame shape
findings.statement: In the reported images, n-butane cool flames had a broader reaction zone than hot flames, while hot flames were more spherical and less attached to the burner tube.
findings.source_quote: While a flame sheet is clearly indicated in the hot flame image, the intensity of a cool flame gradually decreases from the peak along radial direction, which implies that the reaction zone of the cool flame is broader than that of the hot flame. In addition, it is noted that the hot flame is more spherical and less attached to the burner tube than the cool flame.

findings.conditions_text: Due to microgravity
findings.statement: In microgravity, soot in nitrogen-diluted butane flames remains in the flame longer and forms clusters.
findings.source_quote: Due to microgravity, the soot remains in the flame longer and forms clusters.

findings.statement: Escaping soot clusters from a nitrogen-diluted ethane flame can increase heat loss, locally quench the flame, and create holes that permit direct fuel-oxygen mixing and enhance flammability; the flame then reforms and the process can repeat.
findings.safety_implication: Localized quenching should not be treated as proof of extinction because the resulting opening can allow fuel and oxidizer to mix and the flame to reform.
findings.equipment_implication: Crew and automated response procedures should distinguish local flame holes or quenching from confirmed extinction.
findings.source_quote: The escaping soot clusters exacerbate the heat loss experienced by the flame and cause it to locally quench, creating a hole in the flame. This hole allows for direct mixing of the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, thereby enhancing flammability. As a result, the flame reforms, closing the hole, but it opens again due to heat loss.

findings.conditions_text: 12% ethane; 6% ethane
findings.statement: In inverse flames in an ethane/nitrogen chamber, flames in 12% ethane burned longer than flames in 6% ethane.
findings.source_quote: We observed that flames in 12% ethane burned longer than those in 6% ethane.

findings.conditions_text: same oxygen flow rate; greater nitrogen flow rate on the right; chamber filled to 3 atm with propane and nitrogen
findings.statement: In inverse flames, flame size depends on oxygen availability, the limiting reactant; with equal oxygen flow rates, propane/nitrogen flames at 3 atm had similar sizes despite different nitrogen flow rates.
findings.source_quote: This image compares two CFI-G inverse flames that had the same oxygen flow rate, but where the flame on the right had a greater nitrogen flow rate, making the oxygen more dilute and the total flow rate greater. The chamber had been filled to 3 atm with propane and nitrogen. The flames, photographed with an intensified camera, are similar in size.

findings.conditions_text: oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and Combustion Chamber pressure were consistent
findings.statement: For inverse flames with the same oxygen/nitrogen ratio, propane concentration, and chamber pressure, greater oxidizer flow rates produced larger flames; the larger flames were dimmer because radiative heat loss scales with flame size.
findings.source_quote: As such, the tests with the greater oxidizer flow rates result in larger flames. Radiative heat loss scales with flame size, and the larger flames are dimmer than the smaller flames.

findings.conditions_text: inverse flames; oxidizer flow rate from the burner varied
findings.statement: For inverse butane flames, increasing oxidizer flow from the burner produced a larger flame with greater radiative heat loss; radiation from the larger flame was several times greater than from the smaller flame.
findings.source_quote: In these tests, the flame size depends on the amount of fuel in the atmosphere required to consume the oxygen, so a larger flow rate results in a larger flame. However, a flame’s radiative heat loss increases with its size and the larger flame is significantly dimmer. Measurements of thermal radiation from the flame on the right were several times greater than from the flame on the left.

findings.conditions_text: 14.0% and 17.5% butane; same oxidizer mixture ratio and flow rate
findings.statement: In inverse butane flames, the flame at 14.0% butane developed heat-loss-driven oscillations that grew until it self-extinguished, while oscillations in the 17.5% butane flame did not cause extinction during the test.
findings.source_quote: The dim flame in the 14.0% butane experienced large oscillations (shown in blue on the graph) due to heat loss to the burner’s supply tube. These oscillations grew in strength until the flame self-extinguished. In contrast, the flame in 17.5% butane was much brighter.

findings.statement: The investigation describes a cool flame as burning at about 600 degrees Celsius, compared with a candle at around 1,400 degrees Celsius.
findings.source_quote: A cool flame is one that burns at about 600 degrees Celsius. A candle is about two times hotter, burning at around 1,400 degrees Celsius.
findings.earth_application: The report says the investigation's results could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines.
